pedagogy.summary: This topic gives children the roll-call of the solar system: the eight planets named in order from the Sun (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune), the fact that Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006, and the big organising split — four small rocky inner planets and four large gas-giant outer planets. At 7–9 the aim is secure naming/ordering plus that one structural pattern (rocky-then-gassy, small-then-huge), not deep planetary science. Order-from-the-Sun is best learned with a memorable mnemonic AND a spatial model so the sequence isn't just a word-chain but a map. The inner/outer rocky/gas distinction is the first real classification move and should be taught as a noticing ('the four nearest are small and solid; the four far ones are giant balls of gas'). The Pluto story is a lovely hook into how science reclassifies things when definitions sharpen — handled lightly. Keep scale honest in passing (the outer giants are enormously bigger and farther) without turning this into the scale topic.
bestPractices: Pair a mnemonic with a spatial model: a memorable sentence for the order (e.g. 'My Very Easy Method Just Speeds Up Naming') alongside a laid-out Sun-to-Neptune line, so order is both verbal and mapped
Teach the inner/outer split as a noticing: sort the eight into 'small & rocky, close to the Sun' vs 'giant & gassy, far out' and have children justify placements
Tell the Pluto reclassification as a science story: definitions were sharpened in 2006 and Pluto became a 'dwarf planet' — an example of science updating its categories, not a mistake
Use lots of ordering practice (drag-to-order, walk-the-line) since secure sequence from the Sun is the core recall target

Mention scale honestly but lightly (giants dwarf the rocky planets; the gaps grow outward) to avoid the evenly-spaced-same-size mental model, while leaving the full scale treatment to the dedicated later topic
keyRepresentations: A Sun-to-Neptune ordered line/model of the eight planets (the canonical order map)
An order mnemonic sentence paired with the planet names
A two-group sort: rocky inner four vs gas-giant outer four
A relative-size line-up (rocky planets small, giants large) to seed the inner/outer contrast
commonMisconceptions: Pluto is still a planet / was 'demoted by mistake' (it was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006 when the definition of 'planet' was sharpened)
The planets are evenly spaced and similar in size (the outer giants are vastly bigger and the gaps grow enormously outward)
The order can start anywhere / Earth is first or in the middle (order is fixed FROM THE SUN: Mercury first, Earth third)
All planets are solid like Earth (the four outer giants are huge balls of gas/ice with no solid surface to stand on)
There are nine (or more) planets, or the Sun/Moon are planets (there are eight planets; the Sun is a star, the Moon orbits Earth)

learn.summary: For ages 7–9, this topic secures naming and ordering the eight planets from the Sun (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune), the fact that Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006, and one structural pattern: four small rocky inner planets then four large gas-giant outer planets. Pair a memorable mnemonic with a laid-out spatial model so order is both verbal and mapped, teach the inner/outer split as a 'noticing' children justify, and tell the Pluto story as science sharpening its definitions rather than a mistake. Keep scale honest but light, leaving full scale treatment to a dedicated later topic.

activities.title: Walk the Sun-to-Neptune line
feedback: If a learner starts the order from Earth or the middle, remind them the sequence is fixed from the Sun: Mercury is first, Earth is third.
If a learner places a gas giant near the Sun, re-sort together: the small rocky four (Mercury–Mars) are the inner, close planets; the giant gassy four (Jupiter–Neptune) are the outer, far ones.
If a learner thinks all planets are solid like Earth, point out the four outer giants are huge balls of gas/ice with no solid surface to stand on.
Praise correct justifications, e.g. 'Jupiter is a gas giant and it's far out, so it goes in the outer band.'
activities.rationale: Curriculum guidance lists the eight planets in order from the Sun and the rocky-inner/gas-outer distinction; pairing a verbal mnemonic with a spatial layout is intended to support both recall of the fixed sequence and the first classification move. This is a research-informed proposal, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: England's Year 5 'Earth and space' non-statutory guidance lists the eight planets in order from the Sun (Mercury to Neptune), notes Pluto's 2006 reclassification as a dwarf planet, and treats the Sun-centred solar system — the standard primary content for naming and ordering planets.

The solar system consists of the Sun and objects held in orbit around it, including the eight planets; the four inner planets are small and rocky (terrestrial) while the four outer planets are gas/ice giants.
learnerActions: Lay out (on a long paper strip, a hallway floor, or a laid-out line of cards) the eight planets starting at the Sun and moving outward.
Touch each planet in turn and say its name and its position number: Mercury (1), Venus (2), Earth (3), Mars (4), Jupiter (5), Saturn (6), Uranus (7), Neptune (8).
For each planet, say or place a label 'ROCKY' or 'GAS GIANT', and notice that the four near the Sun are small and solid while the four far out are enormous and gassy.
Learn and recite an order mnemonic (e.g. 'My Very Easy Method Just Speeds Up Naming') and then rebuild the line from memory.
Shade or mark a band around the inner four versus the outer four so the split is visible, and describe the widening gap between the rocky worlds and the giants.
activities.intendedInsight: The eight planets have a fixed order FROM THE SUN, and that order carries a real pattern — the four nearest are small and rocky, the four farthest are giants made mostly of gas (Uranus and Neptune also contain a lot of icy material) with no solid surface — not just a word-chain to memorise.

activities.title: Rebuild the order and sort rocky vs gas giant
feedback: On a wrong position, prompt the mnemonic or the position-number check rather than giving the answer outright.
On a wrong sort, ask: is this planet small and solid and near the Sun, or huge and gassy and far out?
If Pluto is placed among the eight, confirm it is still orbiting the Sun but was reclassified in 2006, so it is a dwarf planet, not one of the eight.
activities.rationale: Active retrieval (rebuilding the sequence) and sorting are intended to consolidate the ordered roll-call and the inner/outer classification after guided exploration; both are crisply checkable. Note that a sort can check classification but does not by itself elicit unaided recall of the order, so the unscaffolded rebuild step is included.
sourceClaims: The solar system consists of the Sun and objects held in orbit around it, including the eight planets; the four inner planets are small and rocky (terrestrial) while the four outer planets are gas/ice giants.
learnerActions: From a shuffled set of planet names or cards, place them back into the correct sequence from the Sun, checking each against the ordered line.
Sort the same eight into two groups: 'small & rocky, close to the Sun' versus 'giant & gassy, far out', and say why each belongs.
Add an 'is Pluto a planet?' decision: place Pluto into a separate 'dwarf planet' category and explain the choice.
Do repeated rounds of ordering until the sequence can be rebuilt confidently without the model.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure, independent recall of the planet order and confident classification of each planet as rocky inner or gas-giant outer, with Pluto correctly set aside as a dwarf planet.

activities.title: The Pluto story: when scientists sharpened the rule
feedback: If a learner says Pluto was destroyed, blew up, or flew out of the solar system, correct this directly: Pluto is still orbiting the Sun exactly as before; only the naming rule changed in 2006, and it is now called a dwarf planet.

If a learner insists there are nine planets with Pluto among them, explain there are eight planets plus several dwarf planets (such as Pluto, Ceres and Eris). Finding other far-away icy bodies like Eris helped lead scientists to write the clearer 2006 definition, and better telescopes are why more possible dwarf planets keep being found.
Reinforce the 'why': Pluto is very small and shares its region of space with many other similar icy bodies, so under the sharper rule it counts as a dwarf planet.
activities.rationale: A common misconception treats Pluto's removal as a physical event rather than a reclassification; telling it as a science-definition story is intended to address that and to model how science refines categories. The Pluto reclassification is supported by the verified curriculum source; the precise IAU 'cleared its orbital neighbourhood' definition is drawn from a source marked unverified in the original row and is flagged accordingly.
sourceClaims: England's Year 5 'Earth and space' non-statutory guidance lists the eight planets in order from the Sun (Mercury to Neptune), notes Pluto's 2006 reclassification as a dwarf planet, and treats the Sun-centred solar system — the standard primary content for naming and ordering planets.
learnerActions: Discuss or read the short Pluto story: Pluto was once called the ninth planet; in 2006 scientists made the definition of 'planet' clearer and reclassified Pluto as a dwarf planet.
Answer the diagnostic question: 'Pluto isn't one of the eight anymore. Did Pluto get destroyed, or fly away, or did something else happen? Tell me WHY it's no longer on the list.'
Explain in your own words that Pluto is still out there orbiting the Sun, exactly as before — only the naming rule changed.
Explore the follow-up: could there be other dwarf planets besides Pluto? (e.g. Ceres, Eris) and why scientists keep finding more.
activities.intendedInsight: Science updates its categories when definitions are sharpened. Pluto's change was a change of classification, not a physical event — Pluto is still orbiting the Sun.

constraints: Keep the goal to secure naming, ordering and one classification pattern — not deep planetary science.

Mention scale honestly but lightly (giants dwarf the rocky planets; gaps grow outward) to avoid an evenly-spaced-same-size mental model, while leaving full scale treatment to the dedicated later topic.
A laid-out line or tap-to-reveal model is a strong scaffold for guided exploration, but learners should also rebuild the order independently from memory so recall is not propped up by the display.
Sorting and recognition tasks can check classification but do not by themselves show a learner can state the order unaided; include an unscaffolded recall step.
Teach the Pluto reclassification as a change of definition, not a mistake and not a physical event (destruction/escape).
Correct the inner/outer split firmly: the near four are small and rocky, the far four are the large gas giants — never place gas giants near the Sun.
Present the precise IAU 'planet' definition only with the caveat that it is unverified in the source row; the reclassification fact itself is supported.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original row marks the IAU 2006 'cleared its orbital neighbourhood' definition claim as verified:false. The reclassification of Pluto is supported by the verified curriculum source, but the precise formal definition should be confirmed against the IAU resolution before relying on it verbatim. The simplified child-facing phrasing ('shares its region of space with similar icy bodies') also appears in the source row's assessment correctAnswer.

The original listed a 3D fly-through and open conversation as poor fits with universal-sounding justifications ('open dialogue adds reading load'; '3D is overkill'); these are softened — a brief discussion can usefully support the Pluto reasoning, and a 3D model belongs to the later scale topic rather than being inherently valueless. These are observable-affordance/scope points, not evidence of medium superiority.
Dwarf-planet examples (Ceres, Eris) come from the assessment field of the source row and are included for the enrichment question only; confirm as needed.
Efficacy wording in the rationales was qualified to 'intended to' because no source verifies the effectiveness of the proposed methods.

probeDeeper: Is Pluto still out there in space right now, or has it gone?
Which planets are the small rocky ones, and which are the big gas giants?
Why do you think scientists needed to make a clear rule about what counts as a planet?
Could there be other dwarf planets we've found besides Pluto?
assess.correctAnswer: The eight planets in order from the Sun are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune. Pluto was not destroyed and did not fly away — it is still out there orbiting the Sun. In 2006 scientists changed the DEFINITION of a planet and reclassified Pluto as a 'dwarf planet' because it is very small and shares its region of space with many other similar icy bodies. The four inner planets (Mercury–Mars) are small and rocky; the four outer ones (Jupiter–Neptune) are large gas giants.

errorPatterns.pattern: Pluto was destroyed, blew up, or flew out of the solar system
errorPatterns.nextMove: Clarify Pluto is still orbiting the Sun exactly as before — only the naming rule changed in 2006; it's now called a dwarf planet.
errorPatterns.distractor: Pluto isn't a planet anymore because it was destroyed or flew out of the solar system.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child explains Pluto's removal as a physical event rather than a change of classification

errorPatterns.pattern: the big gas giants are the ones closest to the Sun ('the inner planets are the huge ones')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sort the eight into small-rocky-inner (Mercury–Mars) versus large-gas-giant-outer (Jupiter–Neptune) with pictures to scale.
errorPatterns.distractor: The four planets closest to the Sun are the big gas giants.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child reverses the inner/outer split, placing gas giants near the Sun or rocky planets far out

errorPatterns.pattern: Pluto is still one of the main planets, so there are nine
errorPatterns.nextMove: There are eight planets plus several dwarf planets (Pluto, Ceres, Eris…); explain the 2006 change and why more dwarf planets keep being found.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child lists nine planets, keeping Pluto among them

responseLevels.gap: Explains Pluto's removal as a physical event, or scrambles the order/inner-outer split badly.
responseLevels.full: Lists the eight in order, explains Pluto was reclassified in 2006 (still orbiting, rule changed), and correctly splits small rocky inner planets from large gas-giant outer planets.
responseLevels.partial: Gets much of the order and knows Pluto is a dwarf planet, but explains the change vaguely or muddles which planets are rocky versus gas.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put the planets in order from the Sun as best you can. Now — Pluto used to be called the ninth planet, but it isn't one of the eight anymore. Did Pluto get destroyed, or fly away, or did something else happen? Tell me WHY it's no longer on the list.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who imagines a physical event says Pluto blew up or left. A child who understands the reclassification says Pluto is still there but scientists changed what counts as a planet. The order + inner/outer tiers also catch the common muddle of putting gas giants near the Sun. The 'why' tier separates 'something happened to Pluto' from 'we changed the rule'.
